pages.summary: An array of zeros.
body: The usual way to make room for a result before a loop fills it in: an array made at its final size is faster than one that grows a column at a time. A single size `n` gives a square n-by-n matrix; give `1, n` for a row.
syntax: The sizes as one vector, such as the result of `size`.
Zeros of another class: `'single'`, `'int32'`, `'uint8'` and the other integer classes, or `'logical'`.
Zeros of the class (and complexity) of `p`.
inputs: The sizes. A size of 0 gives an empty array.
The class of the result; `'double'` when not given.

examples.title: A row, a column and a matrix
examples.code:
r = zeros(1, 4)
c = zeros(3, 1)
M = zeros(2)

examples.title: Room for a result filled in a loop

pages.summary: An array of ones.
body: Often a starting point to scale: `5*ones(2, 3)` is a 2-by-3 array of fives (as is `repmat(5, 2, 3)`). A single size `n` gives a square matrix.
syntax: Ones of another class, such as `'single'` or `'uint8'`.

examples.title: Ones, and a constant made from them
A column of ones beside data, for a straight-line fit
examples.intro: The least-squares line through the points is the solution of `[x 1] \ y`.

pages.summary: The identity matrix: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere.
body: `eye(n)` leaves any n-by-n matrix unchanged under multiplication: `A*eye(n)` is `A`. It also starts many matrix expressions, such as `A - lambda*eye(n)`.
syntax: An m-by-n matrix with ones on its main diagonal.

examples.title: The identity, and a rectangular one
Shifting the diagonal of a matrix

pages.summary: Random numbers drawn evenly from the open interval (0, 1).
body: Every value between 0 and 1 is equally likely. For another interval scale and shift: `a + (b - a)*rand(...)` is even on (a, b). The numbers come from a Mersenne Twister generator; `rng` sets its seed, so that a run can be repeated. `rng default` gives the generator's usual first numbers.

examples.title: Estimating pi from random points
examples.intro: The share of points in the unit square that fall inside the quarter circle is close to pi/4.

pages.summary: Random numbers from the standard normal distribution (mean 0, standard deviation 1).
body: For a normal distribution with mean `mu` and standard deviation `sigma`, scale and shift: `mu + sigma*randn(...)`. The generator is the one `rand` and `randi` use, and `rng` seeds it.

examples.title: Mean and spread of a large sample

pages.summary: Random integers drawn evenly from a range.
body: Every integer of the range is equally likely: 1 to `imax`, or `imin` to `imax`. Useful for dice, random indices and shuffles (see also `randperm`).

pages.summary: Seed the random number generator, or read and restore its state.
body: `rand`, `randn`, `randi` and `randperm` share one generator. Setting its seed makes the numbers that follow the same each time a program runs; saving its state with `s = rng` and restoring it with `rng(s)` repeats a stretch of numbers.
syntax: Start the generator from a nonnegative integer seed.
Start from the default seed (0), as a fresh session does.
Seed from the clock, for numbers that differ from run to run.
The generator's settings and state, as a struct.
Put back a state saved earlier.

examples.title: The same numbers again
examples.code:
rng(42)
a = rand(1, 3)
rng(42)
b = rand(1, 3)
isequal(a, b)

examples.title: Saving and restoring the state
examples.code:
rng default
s = rng;
x1 = randn(1, 2)
rng(s)
x2 = randn(1, 2)

pages.summary: Points evenly spaced between two values, both ends included.
body: Unlike the colon operator, which is given a step, `linspace` is given the number of points and always reaches the end exactly. It is the usual way to make the x values of a smooth plot.
inputs: The first and last points; `b` may be less than `a`.
How many points. With `n` 1 the result is `b`.

examples.title: Descending, and many points for a smooth curve
examples.code:
d = linspace(10, 0, 6)
x = linspace(-2, 2, 200);
plot(x, x.^3 - 2*x)
grid on

pages.summary: Vectors of evenly stepped values: a:b and a:step:b.
body: `a:b` counts from `a` up to `b` in steps of 1; `a:step:b` uses another step, which may be negative or not whole. The vector stops at the last value that does not pass `b`, so `b` itself appears only when the steps land on it. Inside an index a lone `:` means every element (`A(:, 2)` is the second column), and `A(:)` is every element as one column.
syntax: a, a+step, …, up to `b` (down to it when `step` is negative).
The same as `a:b`, as a function.

examples.title: Counting up, in steps and down
A range that does not land on its end, and an empty one
examples.output:
d =

     1     3     5     7

e =

  1×0 empty double row vector

examples.title: The colon in an index

pages.summary: Repeat an array as tiles.
body: `repmat(A, m, n)` lays `m` copies of `A` down and `n` across. For arithmetic with a row or a column, implicit expansion often makes copies unnecessary: `A - mean(A)` subtracts each column's mean without `repmat`.
syntax: `m` copies down, `n` across (and more along further dimensions).

examples.title: A constant array, and repeated text

pages.summary: Coordinate arrays for a grid: x varies along the rows, y down the columns.
body: Given the x values of the grid's columns and the y values of its rows, `meshgrid` gives two matrices of the same size holding each point's x and y. A function of x and y can then be computed at every point at once, element by element, and drawn with `surf`, `mesh` or `contour`.
syntax: `X` repeats the row `x` down `length(y)` rows; `Y` repeats the column `y` across `length(x)` columns.

examples.title: A function over a grid, as a surface

pages.summary: The length of each dimension.
body: The size of a matrix is its number of rows and its number of columns; arrays of more dimensions have a length for each. A scalar is 1-by-1, and an empty matrix has at least one length of 0.
syntax: A row: the length of each dimension.
The rows and columns as two outputs (the last output takes the product of any dimensions left over).

examples.title: Rows and columns
Looping over the rows of a matrix
examples.output:
row 1 sums to 15
row 2 sums to 15
row 3 sums to 15

pages.summary: The number of elements.
body: The product of the lengths of all dimensions: the number of values in a numeric array, of cells in a cell array, of structs in a struct array.

examples.title: Looping over every element

pages.summary: The length of the largest dimension (0 for an empty array).
body: For a vector it is the number of elements. For a matrix it is the larger of its row and column counts, which is rarely what is wanted: use `size` with a dimension there.

pages.summary: True when an array has no elements.
body: An array is empty when one of its lengths is 0: `[]`, `''`, `{}`, `zeros(0, 3)`. A string `""` is not empty (it is one string, of no characters); test it with `strlength`.

examples.title: Empty and not
examples.output:
ans =

  logical

   1

ans =

  logical

   1

ans =

  logical

   0

ans =

  logical

   1

examples.title: Searching, and what comes back when nothing is found

pages.summary: The same elements, in the same column order, in another shape.
body: The elements are taken in column order (down the first column, then the next) and laid out again in the new shape, so the number of elements must stay the same. One size may be given as `[]`, and is then worked out from the others.
syntax: An m-by-n (by …) array of the elements of `A`.
`m` rows, and as many columns as the elements fill.

examples.title: Column order
examples.intro: The elements fill the columns first, so a transpose gives them by rows.

pages.summary: Join arrays along a dimension.
body: `[A, B]` (or `[A B]`) joins side by side, as `horzcat` does, and needs the same number of rows; `[A; B]` joins one under the other, as `vertcat` does, and needs the same number of columns. `cat(3, A, B)` stacks matrices along the third dimension. Text joins the same way: `['abc', 'de']` is `'abcde'`.

examples.title: Side by side and one under the other
Building a result row by row

pages.summary: Make a diagonal matrix from a vector, or take a diagonal of a matrix.
body: Given a vector, `diag` builds a square matrix with the vector on a diagonal and zeros elsewhere; given a matrix, it reads a diagonal out as a column. `k` picks the diagonal: 0 is the main one, positive values are above it and negative values below.
syntax: A square matrix with `v` on its main diagonal.
The main diagonal of `A`, as a column.

examples.title: Building and reading diagonals
examples.code:
D = diag([1 2 3])
U = diag([7 8], 1)
A = magic(4);
d = diag(A)'

examples.title: A tridiagonal matrix
examples.code:
n = 5;
T = diag(2*ones(1, n)) + diag(-ones(1, n-1), 1) + diag(-ones(1, n-1), -1)

pages.summary: A random permutation of 1 to n.
body: Every ordering of 1, 2, …, n is equally likely. With `k`, the first `k` of such an ordering: `k` different integers from 1 to n. It is the usual way to shuffle the rows of a matrix, or to draw without replacement.
syntax: The integers 1 to n in random order.

examples.title: A shuffle, and a draw without replacement
examples.code:
rng default
p = randperm(6)
q = randperm(49, 6)

examples.title: Shuffling the rows of a matrix

pages.summary: Points evenly spaced in the exponent, from 10^a to 10^b.
body: The exponents are evenly spaced, as `linspace` spaces them; the points themselves are `10.^linspace(a, b, n)`. Frequencies, scales of rates and other quantities over several orders of magnitude are sampled this way, and look evenly spaced on a logarithmic axis.

examples.title: A response over three decades
examples.code:
f = logspace(0, 3, 200);
semilogx(f, 1 ./ sqrt(1 + (f/50).^2))
grid on
xlabel('frequency')

pages.summary: A magic square: its rows, columns and both diagonals have the same sum.
body: An n-by-n matrix of the integers 1 to n^2 for n of 3 or more, each row, column and diagonal summing to n(n^2 + 1)/2. Handy as a small test matrix whose values are easy to recognize.

pages.summary: Repeat each element of an array.
body: Unlike `repmat`, which repeats the whole array, `repelem` repeats each element in place: `repelem([1 2], 3)` is `[1 1 1 2 2 2]`. A vector of counts gives each element its own number of copies.
syntax: Each element of the vector `v` repeated `n` times (or `n(k)` times for a vector of counts).
Each element of the matrix `A` made an r1-by-r2 block.

examples.title: Each element, and counts of their own

pages.summary: Apply a two-input function with singleton dimensions expanded.
body: Calls the function on arrays whose sizes agree or are 1, the dimensions of length 1 stretched to match: a column against a row gives a matrix. The arithmetic operators do this by themselves (implicit expansion), so `A - mean(A)` needs no `bsxfun`; it remains useful for a function of your own.

examples.title: Centring the columns, both ways

pages.summary: Coordinate arrays for a grid, in the order of the dimensions (the first input varies down the columns).
body: Like `meshgrid`, but the first input runs along the first dimension (down the rows) and the second along the second: the layout `interpn`, `griddedInterpolant` and arrays indexed `A(i, j)` expect. For two inputs the results are the transposes of `meshgrid`'s.
syntax: `X1` varies down the columns, `X2` across the rows.

pages.summary: Logical true or false, or arrays of them.
body: Logical values are what comparisons give; they take one byte each and index arrays by position (`A(mask)`). `true(m, n)` and `false(m, n)` make logical arrays, for example a mask to be filled in.
syntax: An m-by-n logical array of true.
An m-by-n logical array of false.

examples.title: A mask filled in, then used as an index

pages.summary: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
body: The double closest to π, 3.141592653589793. It is a function, so a variable named `pi` hides it.

pages.summary: The distance from a number to the next larger floating-point number.
body: `eps` is 2^-52, about 2.2e-16: the spacing of doubles near 1, and the relative precision of double arithmetic. `eps(x)` is the spacing at `x`, larger for larger numbers. Comparisons of computed values use a tolerance in these terms rather than `==`.
syntax: The spacing at 1 in single precision, 2^-23.

examples.title: Spacing grows with the numbers
examples.code:
e1 = eps
e1000 = eps(1000)
e16 = eps(1e16)
eps('single')

pages.summary: Positive infinity (-Inf for negative), or an array of it.
body: What overflow and division of a nonzero number by zero give. `Inf` compares larger than every finite number, so it serves as a start value for a minimum search and as an unbounded limit (`integral(f, 0, Inf)`). `Inf - Inf` and `0*Inf` are `NaN`.

examples.title: Where infinity comes from, and what it does
examples.output:
ans =

   Inf  -Inf   Inf

ans =

  logical

   1

ans =

   NaN   NaN

examples.title: A start value for a minimum

pages.summary: Not-a-Number, the result of an undefined operation such as 0/0, or an array of it.
body: `NaN` marks a value that is missing or undefined. Arithmetic with it gives `NaN`, and it is not equal to anything, itself included: test for it with `isnan`, never with `==`. Many statistics take `'omitnan'` to leave it out.

examples.title: Where it comes from, and how to find it
examples.code:
[0/0, Inf - Inf]
x = [1 NaN 3];
x == NaN
isnan(x)
examples.output:
ans =

   NaN   NaN

ans =

  1×3 logical array

   0   0   0

ans =

  1×3 logical array

   0   1   0

examples.title: Room for results not yet known

pages.summary: The imaginary unit, the square root of -1.
body: Written after a number, as in `3 + 4i` or `2j`, it makes a complex constant. Alone, `i` and `j` are functions giving the unit, but they are often used as loop variables, which then hide them: `4i` and `1i` always mean the unit.

examples.title: A loop variable named i, and 1i still the unit

pages.summary: The largest and smallest values an integer class holds.
body: Each integer class holds a fixed range: `int8` from -128 to 127, `uint8` from 0 to 255, and so on up to 64 bits. Without a class name, `int32`. Integer arithmetic stops at these limits (it saturates) instead of wrapping round.
syntax: The largest value of another class, such as `'uint8'` or `'int64'`.
The smallest value of another class.

examples.title: The ranges of some classes
examples.output:
ans =

  1×2 int8 row vector

   -128    127

ans =

  uint16

   65535

ans =

  int64

   9223372036854775807

pages.summary: The largest finite and the smallest positive normalized floating-point numbers.
body: `realmax` is about 1.8e308 for double; anything larger overflows to `Inf`. `realmin` is about 2.2e-308, the smallest double with full precision (smaller numbers down to about 4.9e-324 exist with fewer digits). `'single'` gives the limits of single precision.

examples.title: The limits, and past them
examples.code:
big = realmax
small = realmin
realmax * 2
realmax('single')

pages.summary: The largest integer up to which floating point holds every integer exactly (2^53 for double).
body: Every integer up to `flintmax` (9007199254740992 for double) is a double exactly; past it, doubles are two apart, then four, so some integers have no double of their own. Integer counts above it belong in `int64` or `uint64`.

examples.title: The last exact integer
examples.code:
f = flintmax;
fprintf('%.0f\n', f)
f + 1 == f
f - 1 == f
flintmax('single')

pages.summary: A block diagonal matrix built from the matrices given.
body: The matrices go down the diagonal in order, each in its own rows and columns, with zeros elsewhere.

pages.summary: A Toeplitz matrix: constant along each diagonal.
body: The first column is `c` and the first row is `r`; every diagonal repeats its first element. With one argument the matrix is symmetric (Hermitian for complex values). Toeplitz matrices describe convolution and the covariances of a stationary series.
syntax: First column `c`, first row `r` (`c(1)` is used where they meet).

examples.title: Symmetric, and from a column and a row

pages.summary: A Hankel matrix: constant along each anti-diagonal.
body: The first column is `c`; with `r`, the last row is `r`, and without it the matrix is zero below the anti-diagonal. Each anti-diagonal (running up to the right) repeats one value.
syntax: First column `c`, zeros below the anti-diagonal.

pages.summary: The Vandermonde matrix of a vector: its columns are powers of the vector.
body: Column j is `v.^(n-j)`, so the last column is ones. Solving with it fits the polynomial through the points (`polyfit` does this more stably).
syntax: The Vandermonde matrix, highest power first.

pages.summary: The Hilbert matrix, H(i,j) = 1/(i+j-1), and its exact inverse.
body: The Hilbert matrix is a classic example of an ill-conditioned matrix: its condition number grows very fast with its size, so linear systems with it lose digits. `invhilb` gives its inverse exactly (integers), for checking how much a numerical inverse loses.

examples.title: The matrix, its condition, and its inverse
How much a numerical inverse loses

pages.summary: The Pascal matrix: binomial coefficients, symmetric and positive definite.
body: Element (i, j) is the binomial coefficient `nchoosek(i+j-2, j-1)`, so the anti-diagonals are rows of Pascal's triangle. Its determinant is 1 and its inverse has integer entries.

pages.summary: The companion matrix of a polynomial; its eigenvalues are the polynomial's roots.
body: For coefficients `p` (highest power first), a square matrix whose characteristic polynomial is `p`: its eigenvalues are the roots, which is how `roots` finds them.

pages.summary: Eigenvalue test matrices: Wilkinson's, and Rosser's 8-by-8.
body: `wilkinson(n)` is symmetric tridiagonal, with ones beside the diagonal and |k| on it; its largest eigenvalues come in nearly equal pairs, a test for eigenvalue solvers. `rosser` is a symmetric 8-by-8 integer matrix with a double eigenvalue, three nearly equal ones, a zero and a nearly zero one.

pages.summary: Gather values by index and combine those that share one (a sum by default).
body: Each value goes to the place its index (a row of `subs`) names; values sent to the same place are summed, or combined by `fun`. With group numbers as the indices it computes a statistic for each group, as `unique`'s third output gives them.
syntax: Sums of `vals` by the indices in `subs`.
With the size of the result.
Combined by `fun` instead of summed, such as `@max` or `@(x) {x}`.
A = accumarray(subs, vals, sz, fun, fillval)
inputs: subs — matrix, vector or cell array of index vectors
A column for each dimension of the result (a column of positions for a vector result).
The values, one for each row of `subs` (a scalar goes to every one).

examples.title: Counting and summing by group
The largest value of each group, and an empty group
A table of counts from two indices
